list.listitem: Dupuytren's contracture is a clinical diagnosis characterized by shortening and thickening of the palmar fascia aponeurosis typically resulting in flexion contracture of the 4th and 5th digits. C
Steroid injections into early Dupuytren's nodules may reduce the need for surgery. C
Collegenase clostridium histolyticum injection is an FDA-approved alternative to surgical treatment of moderate to severe Dupuytren's contracture. B
Indications for surgical intervention include metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joint contracture greater than 30 degrees and any degree of proximal interphalangeal (PIP) joint contracture. C

background.definition: The condition is marked by fibrosis with a shortening and thickening of the palmar aponeurosis that presents as a flexion contracture of the fingers into the palm of the hand.

list.listitem: The annual incidence is estimated at about 3 cases per 10,000 US adults.
Predominantly elderly men of Northern European descent are affected by Dupuytren's contracture. Incidence increases with age, tobacco or alcohol use, and in patients with diabetes.

The disease is often associated with involvement of other areas of the body: Garrod's knuckle pads (44%-54%), plantar fibromatosis (Ledderhose disease, 6%-31%), and penile fibromatosis (Peyronie's disease, 2%-8%).
The cause is unknown, although there may be an autoimmune component. The evidence suggests a genetic link of autosomal dominance with incomplete penetrance.
Dupuytren's contracture is more common in men, alcohol users, smokers, and diabetics.
Exposure to vibration is an additional risk factor (OR 2.87, 95% CI 1.4-5.8).
Dupuytren's contracture is classified as a fibroproliferative disorder that early on manifests clinically as a nodule.
With disease progression the connective tissue assembles and manifests clinically as a cord.
Myofibroblasts are prominent in Dupuytren's tissue and their contractile nature contribute to contracture of the tissue.
Dupuytren's contracture is a clinical diagnosis. C
Skin changes, such as puckering of tissue over flexor tendon, are an early sign of the disease. C
Nodules, typically painless, develop before cords and contracture occur. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Nodule from the tendon sheath and does not form cords or dimple skin
Pain and triggering secondary to tenosynovitis, can manually straighten into extension unlike advanced Dupuytren's
History of trauma and no prior history of nodules in affected digit
Acute forearm muscle injury causes ischemia. Deformity of wrist, hand, fingers. Poor blood flow on exam
Nonprogressive, no family history, without gender predilection, unilateral
Cords not characteristic,limited joint mobility typically involving all fingers; Dupuytren's typically involves the fourth and fifth digits
Often associated with malignancy. Typically involves all fingers on both hands; Dupuytrens typically involved fourth and fifth digits

list.listitem: The presenting complaint is often impaired function of the hand as a result of the contracture when it begins to affect workplace or home activities. The disease typically affects the ring and little fingers but may affect any digit.
Pitting and thickening of the palmar skin are early manifestations. Next a firm, painless nodule typically develops within the deeper palmar fascia.

Nodules, the key diagnostic feature, normally precede the formation of cords and are commonly fixed to the skin and palmar fascia. This cord gradually contracts over months to years, forming the flexion contracture of first the MCP joint and then the PIP joint.
A positive Hueston's tabletop test is when patients are unable to place their palm flat on a tabletop.
No diagnostic (imaging or lab) testing is recommended—this is a clinical diagnosis.

Suspect Dupuytren's contracture in patients with painless stiffness of the fourth and fifth fingers, palmar skin thickening or puckering, SC nodules and cords, and flexion contracture of the MCP joint.
If MCP contracture is greater than 30 degrees or any PIP joint contracture, discuss referral of the patient to a hand surgeon.
Steroid injections into early Dupuytren's nodules may delay progression. C
Collegenase clostridium histolyticum injection is an FDA-approved alternative to surgical treatment of moderate to severe Dupuytren's contracture. B

Needle aponeurotomy (i.e., percutaneous needle fasciotomy) appears as effective as collagenase injections with a lower reintervention rate and is less expensive, but limited fasciectomy is better than collagenase injections. B
Indications for surgical intervention include MCP joint contracture greater than 30 degrees or any degree of PIP joint contracture. C

Clinical trials support perinodular steroid injections every 4 to 6 weeks for up to 5 months may reduce progression of disease, but a systematic review notes the quality of the evidence is low and more studies are needed to draw definitive conclusions.

A RCT of collagenase clostridium histolyticum (FDA approved) showed improvement in contractures and increased is range of motion over 90 days. In a small (n = 70) open-label trial, patients who received collagenase injections had similar outcomes at 3 years as patients who received percutaneous needle fasciotomy.

Surgery is the mainstay of advanced disease. Indications for surgical intervention include MCP contracture of 30 degrees and any degree of PIP joint contracture. Options include fasciotomy and fasciectomy, with or without percutaneous needle aponeurotomy.
Fasciotomy involves cord division and is performed as either an open procedure or via percutaneous needle fasciotomy.
Limited or radical fasciectomy are removal of the diseased or entire palmar fascia, respectively.
Complex regional pain syndrome may be reduced after fasciectomy for Dupuytren's contracture by using either an auxiliary nerve block or IV regional anesthesia with clonidine.

A Cochrane review showed insufficient evidence is available to show the relative superiority of different surgical procedures (needle fasciotomy vs fasciectomy, or interposition firebreak skin grafting vs z-plasty closure of fasciectomy). Additionally, postoperative splinting may not be helpful and may cause dimished active flexion.

A trial randomized 672 persons to collagenase injections or to surgery with limited fasciectomy. The primary outcome on a 100 point symptom scale where lower scores are better favored limited fasciectomy at one year (17.8 for injection vs 11.9 points for surgery) and 2 years. The researcher's verdict was that collagenase injection was "not non-inferior" to surgery.

Other treatments that have been proposed include passive stretching of affected joint, intralesional interferon gamma injections, hyperbaric oxygen, splinting, topical vitamin A, and even radiotherapy. However, no rigorous trials could be identified in the literature to support these approaches.
Intraoperative 5-fluorouracil has been recommended, but an RCT of 15 patients with each serving also as a control found no benefit after an 18-month follow-up.
Surgical referral is indicated when the MCP joint contraction exceeds 30 degrees or there is any degree of PIP joint contraction.
Many cases of Dupuytren's disease will not develop contractures and may be managed expectantly with yearly follow-up. C
Between 15-20 percent of patients will require surgical intervention, with males having a higher lifetime risk of surgery. B

There have only been 3 histologically confirmed cases of Dupuytren's disease in children 10 years and younger, making this an extremely rare condition. However, it should be included in the differential diagnosis of a nodule in the hand or a contracture of the finger in a pediatric patient.
